Examples include [`CreateDesignReferenceFeatures`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/transforms/design_transforms.py#L117) for generating reference positions and motif token classes, [`FeaturizeAtoms`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/transforms/design_transforms.py#L346) for adding atom-wise properties like RASA and hydrogen bond donor/acceptor states, and [`AddIsXFeats`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/transforms/design_transforms.py#L399) for boolean masks indicating atom types (e.g., backbone, alpha carbon). Noise augmentation, such as [`AugmentNoise`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/transforms/design_transforms.py#L611), is also applied here to enhance the robustness of diffusion models during training.

The framework incorporates specialized transformations for **hydrogen bond calculations**. [`/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/transforms/hbonds.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/transforms/hbonds.py) handles the addition of hydrogen atoms and the calculation of hydrogen bonds using [`biotite`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/.env#L19), while [`/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/transforms/hbonds_hbplus.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/transforms/hbonds_hbplus.py) integrates with the external [`HBPLUS`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/README.md#L143) tool for more sophisticated H-bond analysis. These transforms annotate structures with [`active_donor`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/docs/input.md#L85) and [`active_acceptor`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/docs/input.md#L85) features, which are vital for designing hydrogen bond-mediated interactions.

A key capability for multipolymer design is the handling of **nucleic acid secondary structure**. The [`/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/transforms/na_geom.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/transforms/na_geom.py) and [`/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/transforms/na_geom_utils.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/transforms/na_geom_utils.py) modules compute nucleic acid secondary structure features, including base-pair partners and counts, either from geometric analysis or user-provided specifications like dot-bracket strings. This allows the model to explicitly condition on or generate desired nucleic acid conformations.

**Symmetry operations** are crucial for designing symmetric biomolecular assemblies, and are primarily managed by [`/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/transforms/symmetry.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/transforms/symmetry.py). The [`AddSymmetryFeats`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/transforms/symmetry.py#L10) transform extracts and integrates symmetry-related transformations ([`sym_transform`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/transforms/symmetry.py#L33)) and annotations ([`sym_transform_id`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/transforms/symmetry.py#L22), [`sym_entity_id`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/transforms/symmetry.py#L23), [`is_sym_asu`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/transforms/symmetry.py#L24)) into the data. These features help ensure that generated structures adhere to specified symmetries, maintaining structural integrity across repeated units. Further details on symmetry handling in RFD3NA, including utility functions like [`add_sym_annotations`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/inference/symmetry/atom_array.py#L15) and [`apply_symmetry_to_atomarray_coord`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/inference/symmetry/atom_array.py#L152), can be found in [RFD3NA Multipolymer Contig Specification and Input Selection](#introduction-to-foundry-models-rfd3na-multipolymer-contig-specification-and-input-selection) and [RFD3NA Input Specification and Multipolymer Contigs](#rfdiffusion3na-rfd3na-for-multipolymer-design-rfd3na-input-specification-and-multipolymer-contigs). The tests in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/tests`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/tests) validate these symmetry operations, confirming that atoms are correctly assigned to symmetry mates and that the structural relationships are preserved.

The orchestration of these diverse transformations into coherent pipelines is handled by [`/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/transforms/pipelines.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/transforms/pipelines.py). This module uses constructs like [`Compose`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rigid.py#L626) to sequence transforms, [`ConditionalRoute`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rf3/src/rf3/data/pipelines.py#L42) for executing transforms based on specific conditions (e.g., training vs. inference), and [`RandomRoute`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rf3/src/rf3/data/pipelines.py#L45) for stochastic elements like cropping. This modular design enables flexible and powerful data preparation workflows tailored to various multipolymer design challenges.

### RFD3NA Training Pipeline and Metrics
The RFD3NA training process leverages [`hydra`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/pyproject.toml#L27) for flexible configuration management and [`lightning.fabric`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/examples/all.ipynb#L84) to enable distributed training across multiple GPUs. The primary entry point for initiating training is the [`/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/train.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/train.py) script, which orchestrates the entire workflow from configuration loading to model execution.

The core training logic is encapsulated within the [`AADesignTrainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/trainer/rfd3.py#L33), defined in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/trainer/rfd3na.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/trainer/rfd3na.py). This specialized trainer extends the generic [`FabricTrainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L56) (see [Training Harness with PyTorch Lightning Fabric](#foundry-core-library-and-ml-workflows-training-harness-with-pytorch-lightning-fabric)) to handle the unique aspects of multipolymer design. It manages the assembly of network inputs, the computation of losses during the [`training_step`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L661), and the evaluation of model performance during the [`validation_step`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L681). During training, the [`AADesignTrainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/trainer/rfd3.py#L33) uses a recycling schedule generated by the [`get_recycle_schedule`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rf3/src/rf3/utils/recycling.py#L7) function in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/trainer/recycling.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/trainer/recycling.py) to ensure consistent computational intensity across batches and GPUs. This schedule helps in robustly training diffusion models by varying the number of refinement iterations.

A comprehensive suite of metrics and loss functions guides and evaluates the model's learning. The [`Loss`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/losses.py#L8) class (see [Loss Function Aggregation with the Loss Class](#model-evaluation-metrics-and-loss-functions-loss-function-aggregation-with-the-loss-class)), integrated into the [`AADesignTrainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/trainer/rfd3.py#L33), supports various loss components, including [`SequenceLoss`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/metrics/losses.py#L7) and [`DiffusionLoss`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rf3/src/rf3/loss/af3_losses.py#L416), which can incorporate [`smoothed_lddt_loss`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rf3/src/rf3/loss/af3_losses.py#L544) for structural accuracy. During validation, the model's tensor outputs are transformed into [`AtomArrayStack`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/engine.py#L13) objects using utilities such as [`_build_atom_array_stack`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/trainer/trainer_utils.py#L69) from [`/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/trainer/trainer_utils.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/trainer/trainer_utils.py). These structured outputs are then evaluated using a rich set of metrics found in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/metrics`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/metrics). These metrics include detailed design quality assessments like clash detection, chain break analysis, and backbone metrics from [`/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/metrics/design_metrics.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/metrics/design_metrics.py). For nucleic acid designs, specialized metrics like F1 scores for secondary structure similarity are calculated using [`/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/metrics/nucleic_ss_metrics.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/metrics/nucleic_ss_metrics.py). Hydrogen bond metrics from [`/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/metrics/hbonds_metrics.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/metrics/hbonds_metrics.py) and [`/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/metrics/hbonds_hbplus_metrics.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/metrics/hbonds_hbplus_metrics.py), along with ligand contact metrics from [`/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/metrics/rna_aptamer_metrics.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/metrics/rna_aptamer_metrics.py), are also employed to provide a holistic view of the designed multipolymer structures. The [`DumpValidationStructuresCallback`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/trainer/dump_validation_structures.py#L19) in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/trainer/dump_validation_structures.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/trainer/dump_validation_structures.py) further enhances evaluation by saving predicted structures and associated metadata during validation, allowing for visual inspection and deeper analysis of the design outcomes.

### RFD3NA Inference Engine and Model Architecture
RFdiffusion3NA (RFD3NA) provides a framework for designing complex biomolecular structures involving proteins, DNA, and RNA. The inference engine, primarily managed by [`RFD3InferenceEngine`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/engine.py#L140) in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/engine.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/engine.py), orchestrates the entire design workflow, from handling input specifications to generating and saving multipolymer outputs.

The inference process begins with robust input handling, where [`RFD3InferenceEngine`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/engine.py#L140) processes diverse input formats, including file paths and detailed [`DesignInputSpecification`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/inference/input_parsing.py#L115) objects. This standardization ensures that design constraints, such as defining specific [`contig`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/inference/input_parsing.py#L134) regions (e.g., [`10-10,20-20R,30-30D`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/README.md#L55) for protein, RNA, and DNA chains) or specifying fixed atoms and unindexed areas, are correctly interpreted and prepared for the model. The [`run`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/engine.py#L273) method of [`RFD3InferenceEngine`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/engine.py#L140) then executes the design process by interacting with the underlying diffusion model.

At the core of the design process is the [`RFD3`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/model/RFD3.py#L19) model, defined in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/model/RFD3.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/model/RFD3.py). This model wraps the [`RFD3DiffusionModule`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/model/RFD3_diffusion_module.py#L32), which serves as the generative engine. The [`RFD3DiffusionModule`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/model/RFD3_diffusion_module.py#L32) (found in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/model/RFD3_diffusion_module.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/model/RFD3_diffusion_module.py)) employs a UNet-like architecture to iteratively denoise noisy atomic coordinates and sequence features. It refines predictions through a recycling mechanism, continuously improving the generated structures. The module's design incorporates various neural network building blocks, such as specialized attention mechanisms and token encoders, optimized for biomolecular structure prediction.

The iterative denoising process is guided by the [`ConditionalDiffusionSampler`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/model/inference_sampler.py#L582), implemented in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/model/inference_sampler.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/src/rfd3na/model/inference_sampler.py). This sampler manages the step-by-step refinement of the structure, allowing for controlled diffusion. It supports advanced features like classifier-free guidance, which enables the model to generate diverse designs while adhering to specified conditions by comparing predictions made with and without conditioning information. Furthermore, the sampler can apply symmetry constraints during the diffusion process, ensuring that generated multipolymer structures maintain desired symmetries. The flexibility of the [`ConditionalDiffusionSampler`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/model/inference_sampler.py#L582) extends to incorporating motif alignment and other specific design criteria throughout the sampling trajectory.

### RFD3NA Tutorials and Examples for Multipolymer Design
The [`/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/docs/tutorials`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/docs/tutorials) directory provides practical guides for utilizing RFdiffusion3NA (RFD3NA) to design diverse biomolecular systems, including enzymes, nucleic acid binders, and protein-protein interfaces. These tutorials demonstrate how to configure and execute design tasks, emphasizing the use of JSON or YAML configuration files to define design parameters and constraints.

For **enzyme design**, the [`enzyme_design_tutorial.md`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/docs/index.rst#L28) ([`/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/docs/tutorials/enzyme_design_tutorial.md`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/docs/tutorials/enzyme_design_tutorial.md)) focuses on designing around specific catalytic residues and controlling the protein's interaction with a ligand. Key configuration parameters include [`input`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/inference/input_parsing.py#L132) (PDB file), [`ligand`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/inference/input_parsing.py#L142) identification, [`unindex`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/inference/input_parsing.py#L135) to allow sequence redesign in specified regions, and [`length`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/inference/input_parsing.py#L141) to define the size of the designed protein. [`select_fixed_atoms`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/inference/input_parsing.py#L152) is used to constrain atoms to maintain their positions, while [`select_buried`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/inference/input_parsing.py#L170) and [`select_exposed`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/inference/input_parsing.py#L172) apply RASA (Relative Accessible Surface Area) conditioning to guide ligand interaction. The [`select_unfixed_sequence`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/inference/input_parsing.py#L160) parameter enables sequence optimization for fixed backbone regions, illustrating a design approach that decouples sequence from structure.

The [`na_binder_tutorial.md`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/docs/index.rst#L29) ([`/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/docs/tutorials/na_binder_tutorial.md`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/docs/tutorials/na_binder_tutorial.md)) outlines the process for **nucleic acid binder design**, specifically focusing on DNA-protein complexes. This tutorial introduces the [`contig`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/inference/input_parsing.py#L134) parameter for defining both fixed and *de novo* designed segments, including nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) and protein chains. [`unindex`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/inference/input_parsing.py#L135) allows for "unindexed motifs" whose positions are determined during diffusion, and their placement is tracked using [`diffused_index_map`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/trainer/rfd3.py#L404) in the output. [`select_fixed_atoms`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/inference/input_parsing.py#L152) (e.g., [`BKBN`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/README.md#L90) for backbone only) can be used to stabilize parts of the input structure, while [`is_non_loopy`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/inference/input_parsing.py#L191) encourages designs with minimal loops. Hydrogen bond conditioning can be incorporated using [`select_hbond_acceptor`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/inference/input_parsing.py#L174) and [`select_hbond_donor`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/inference/input_parsing.py#L175) with an external tool like HBPLUS.

For **protein-protein interface (PPI) design**, the [`ppi_design_tutorial.md`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/docs/index.rst#L27) ([`/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/docs/tutorials/ppi_design_tutorial.md`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/docs/tutorials/ppi_design_tutorial.md)) illustrates how to configure RFD3NA to generate protein binders. This tutorial leverages [`select_hotspots`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/inference/input_parsing.py#L176) to define specific residues on the target protein that the designed binder should interact with. The [`infer_ori_strategy: hotspots`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/utils/inference.py#L399) setting places the origin token for the designed protein relative to these hotspots, biasing the diffusion process towards desired interaction sites. Similar to nucleic acid binder design, [`is_non_loopy: true`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/docs/input.md#L70) helps produce less looped structures. The tutorial also highlights a broader design workflow where RFD3NA is followed by other tools for filtering, sequence redesign (e.g., with ProteinMPNN as discussed in [Protein and Ligand Inverse Folding (MPNN)](#protein-and-ligand-inverse-folding-mpnn)), and structure validation (e.g., with RoseTTAFold3, covered in [RoseTTAFold3 (RF3) for Structure Prediction](#rosettafold3-rf3-for-structure-prediction)).

All tutorials use the [`rfd3 design`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/README.md#L1) command-line tool, providing parameters such as [`out_dir`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/examples/all.ipynb#L103) for output location, [`inputs`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/examples/all.ipynb#L102) pointing to the configuration file, and [`ckpt_path`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/engine.py#L45) for specifying model checkpoints. Output analysis involves examining [`.cif.gz`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rf3/README.md#L620) files for structural visualization and [`.json`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/README.md#L67) files for detailed metadata, including [`diffused_index_map`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/trainer/rfd3.py#L404) and [`diffused_com`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/metrics/design_metrics.py#L155) (new origin token location). The system's JSON-based configuration allows for declarative specification of complex design scenarios, from simple protein designs to intricate hybrid designs with specific secondary structure, base-pairing, and ligand-interaction constraints, as further elaborated in [`atom23_design.md`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/README.md#L71) ([`/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/docs/examples/atom23_design.md`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/docs/examples/atom23_design.md)) and the [`input.md`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/README.md#L14) documentation ([`/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/docs/input.md`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3na/docs/input.md)). These examples collectively demonstrate RFD3NA's flexibility in addressing diverse biomolecular design challenges.

## Foundry Core Library and ML Workflows
The Foundry core library provides the foundational infrastructure for machine learning workflows, encompassing configuration management, general utility functions, inference engines, metrics, and training harnesses. This design ensures a structured approach to building and deploying biomolecular design models.

A package-wide initialization process, defined in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/__init__.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/__init__.py), configures global settings. This includes loading environment variables from [`.env`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/.env#L2) files for parameters like debug mode and type checking, and setting up the package-specific logger. Crucially, it manages the integration of GPU acceleration technologies such as [`cuEquivariance`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/README.md#L39) and defines a global flag to disable checkpointing. Dynamic configuration is supported through custom Hydra [`OmegaConf`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/logging.py#L8) resolvers in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/hydra/resolvers.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/hydra/resolvers.py), which allow for importing Python modules and converting enum values to regex strings directly within configuration files.

The framework includes a callback system, detailed in [Machine Learning Callbacks](#machine-learning-callbacks), which provides an extensible mechanism for injecting custom logic at various stages of the training and validation processes. These callbacks enable functionalities such as tracking model health, logging validation metrics, and profiling training performance.

The system incorporates a generic training harness, the [`FabricTrainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L56), built on PyTorch Lightning Fabric. This harness orchestrates the entire training lifecycle, handling accelerator and strategy configuration, managing the model's state, and dynamically constructing models (with support for Exponential Moving Average or EMA), optimizers, and schedulers. It also implements robust training and validation loops, manages gradient accumulation, handles NaN/Inf gradients, and provides a checkpointing mechanism for saving and restoring the model's state.

Essential training utilities complement the [`FabricTrainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L56). The [`EMA`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/training/EMA.py#L9) class in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/training/EMA.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/training/EMA.py) smooths model parameters for improved generalization. Gradient checkpointing techniques, such as [`create_custom_forward`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rf3/src/rf3/util_module.py#L33) and [`activation_checkpointing`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/training/checkpoint.py#L38) in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/training/checkpoint.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/training/checkpoint.py), optimize memory usage during training. Learning rate schedulers, including the [`AF3Scheduler`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/training/schedulers.py#L7) in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/training/schedulers.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/training/schedulers.py), control learning rate adjustments over the training process.

The library offers a comprehensive set of utilities for data, model, and distributed management. Data handling is managed by [`SquashfsManager`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/squashfs.py#L18) in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/squashfs.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/squashfs.py) for lazy mounting of Squashfs filesystems, and the functionality found in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/datasets.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/datasets.py) for distributed data loading and dataset composition. Model weight management, including flexible loading and parameter freezing policies, is provided by the functionality found in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/weights.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/weights.py). Dynamic instantiation of callbacks and loggers is handled by [`instantiate_callbacks`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/instantiators.py#L19) and [`instantiate_loggers`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/instantiators.py#L47) in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/instantiators.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/instantiators.py), while distributed training utilities including [`get_current_rank`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/ddp.py#L12) and [`is_rank_zero`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/ddp.py#L17) in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/ddp.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/ddp.py) facilitate DDP setup, rank management, and XPU acceleration support in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/xpu`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/xpu).

For structural bioinformatics, specialized utilities for geometric and tensor operations are provided. These include [`weighted_rigid_align`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/alignment.py#L8) in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/alignment.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/alignment.py) for point cloud alignment, robust parsing and validation of protein component identifiers via functions like [`split_contig`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/components.py#L48) and [`extract_pn_unit_info`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/components.py#L64) in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/components.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/components.py), and core utilities for 3D rigid transformations through [`Rotation`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rigid.py#L278) and [`Rigid`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rigid.py#L850) classes in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rigid.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rigid.py). Methods for applying geometric augmentation through random rotations and translations are also available via [`get_random_augmentation`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rotation_augmentation.py#L17) and [`uniform_random_rotation`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rotation_augmentation.py#L37) in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rotation_augmentation.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rotation_augmentation.py).

Finally, command-line interface (CLI) tools, described in [Command Line Interface (CLI) Utilities](#command-line-interface-cli-utilities), enable users to manage various aspects of the Foundry ecosystem, such as installing, listing, and cleaning up model checkpoints.

### Core Library Initialization and Dynamic Configuration
The Foundry library performs essential package-wide initialization and configuration to streamline machine learning workflows. This process begins by loading settings from [`.env`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/.env#L2) files and environment variables, utilizing [`environs`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/pyproject.toml#L28) within [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/__init__.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/__init__.py). This dynamic loading mechanism allows for flexible adjustment of behaviors such as enabling runtime type checking ([`TYPE_CHECK`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/__init__.py#L12)), activating debug mode ([`DEBUG`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/__init__.py#L13)), performing NaN checks ([`NAN_CHECK`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/__init__.py#L14)), and controlling the integration of GPU acceleration components like [`cuequivariance_torch`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/pyproject.toml#L63).

A key aspect of this initialization is the conditional enablement of runtime type checking through [`beartype`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/pyproject.toml#L34). If the [`TYPE_CHECK`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/__init__.py#L12) environment variable is set, the system calls [`beartype_this_package`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/__init__.py#L5) and [`install_import_hook`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/__init__.py#L7) to ensure that type annotations are enforced during execution. Similarly, GPU acceleration using [`cuequivariance_torch`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/pyproject.toml#L63) is conditionally integrated based on the availability of CUDA and a [`DISABLE_CUEQUIVARIANCE`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/__init__.py#L35) flag, ensuring that performance-enhancing features are only activated when appropriate. A global [`DISABLE_CHECKPOINTING`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/__init__.py#L54) flag is also set during this phase, providing a universal control for checkpointing behavior across the library.

Beyond basic settings, Foundry leverages custom Hydra resolvers, defined in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/hydra/resolvers.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/hydra/resolvers.py), for dynamic configuration. The [`resolve_import`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/hydra/resolvers.py#L28) resolver enables the dynamic loading of Python modules and their attributes directly from configuration files, which is particularly useful for specifying models, datasets, or other components without hardcoding their paths. Another resolver, [`chain_type_info_to_regex`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/hydra/resolvers.py#L51), dynamically converts [`ChainType`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/hydra/resolvers.py#L9) or [`ChainTypeInfo`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/hydra/resolvers.py#L9) enum values into regular expression strings, allowing for flexible filtering and specification of chain types in various structural design tasks. These resolvers allow complex configurations to be specified declaratively in Hydra, with their values resolved dynamically at runtime.

### Callback System for Training Workflow Automation
Foundry employs a callback system to enable custom logic injection at various stages of the machine learning training and validation processes. This system is structured around the abstract base class [`BaseCallback`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py#L9), defined in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py), which provides a set of hook methods corresponding to different events in the training lifecycle. These hooks allow developers to execute specific actions, such as logging, monitoring, or modifying training behavior, without altering the core training loop. Each hook typically provides access to the [`trainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/mpnn/src/mpnn/train.py#L287) object, allowing interaction with the training state and underlying [`lightning.fabric`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/examples/all.ipynb#L84) components.

Specific implementations of these callbacks address different aspects of training automation:

Model health tracking is handled by the [`ActivationsGradientsWeightsTracker`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/health_logging.py#L48) in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/health_logging.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/health_logging.py). This callback monitors the behavior of a neural network by collecting statistics on its activations, gradients, and weights. It uses hooks to register and remove forward pass captures and iterates through model parameters to gather metrics such as mean, standard deviation, and norm. These statistics can be logged as scalars or histograms, providing insights into model stability and training progression.

For managing validation metrics, the [`StoreValidationMetricsInDFCallback`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/metrics_logging.py#L16) in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/metrics_logging.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/metrics_logging.py) collects and aggregates validation results. In distributed training environments, each process accumulates its own metrics into a DataFrame and saves it to a temporary file. The global rank zero then gathers these files, concatenates them, and stores the combined results, handling potential data duplication. This ensures a consolidated view of validation performance across all distributed nodes.

Performance profiling during training is facilitated by the [`TimingCallback`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/timing_logging.py#L13) in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/timing_logging.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/timing_logging.py). This callback measures the duration of various training phases, such as data loading, forward and backward passes, and optimizer steps. It uses an internal [`Timers`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/torch.py#L330) object to track these durations and reports average timings at configurable intervals, providing insight into where computational resources are being spent.

Comprehensive training progress logging is implemented through several callbacks within [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/train_logging.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/train_logging.py). These include callbacks to log the number of model parameters, display example IDs for debugging, monitor dataset sampling ratios, track learning rates, and provide detailed breakdowns of training losses. These callbacks contribute to a rich console output, offering a clear overview of the training process and resource utilization.

### Training Harness with PyTorch Lightning Fabric
Foundry's generic training harness, [`FabricTrainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L56), is built upon PyTorch Lightning Fabric and orchestrates the entire lifecycle of model training and validation. It is defined in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py). The [`FabricTrainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L56) manages the setup of accelerators and strategies, configuring how training utilizes hardware resources and distributed computing. This includes handling [`XPUAccelerator`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/xpu/xpu_accelerator.py#L9) and [`SingleXPUStrategy`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/xpu/single_xpu_strategy.py#L13) for Intel XPU devices.

The trainer initializes and updates its internal state, which includes the model, optimizer, scheduler configuration, and global training parameters. It dynamically constructs essential components such as the model, optimizers, and learning rate schedulers, often leveraging Hydra for flexible configuration. Support for Exponential Moving Average (EMA) is integrated, allowing models to be wrapped with EMA during construction for improved generalization.

The core of the [`FabricTrainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L56) functionality lies in its training and validation loops. The [`fit`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L329) method orchestrates the overall training process, iterating through epochs and managing checkpoint loading and validation. The [`train_loop`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L510) executes a single training epoch, managing gradient accumulation, stepping the optimizer, and updating the scheduler. Similarly, the [`validation_loop`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L598) runs a single validation epoch, switching the model to evaluation mode, collecting metrics, and then restoring the training mode. Subclasses of [`FabricTrainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L56) implement abstract [`training_step`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L661) and [`validation_step`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L681) methods to define the specific forward and backward passes for each batch.

The [`FabricTrainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L56) also handles optimizer steps, including mechanisms to skip updates if NaN or Inf gradients are detected and applying gradient clipping to prevent exploding gradients. It ensures that EMA parameters are updated when enabled. Robust checkpointing mechanisms are in place for saving and loading the complete trainer state, including model weights, optimizer states, and scheduler configurations. This allows for intelligent restoration of training progress and flexible loading policies, such as freezing specific parameters, as described in [Model Weight Management and Parameter Freezing](#general-utilities-for-deep-learning-infrastructure-model-weight-management-and-parameter-freezing). The [`FabricTrainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L56) also includes utility functions for checking the environment (e.g., interactive mode) and providing rank-zero-only logging to avoid redundant output in distributed settings.

### Training Utilities: EMA, Checkpointing, and Schedulers
The Foundry framework integrates several utilities to enhance and stabilize the training process, complementing the core [`FabricTrainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L56) [Training Harness with PyTorch Lightning Fabric](#foundry-core-library-and-ml-workflows-training-harness-with-pytorch-lightning-fabric). These utilities focus on improving model generalization, optimizing memory usage, and providing flexible control over the learning rate schedule.

For instance, the Exponential Moving Average (EMA) is implemented in the [`EMA`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/training/EMA.py#L9) class within [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/training/EMA.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/training/EMA.py). This mechanism maintains a "shadow" copy of the model's parameters, which are updated as an exponential moving average of the actively trained model's weights. During inference, the shadow model can be used instead of the primary model, often leading to more stable and better-generalizing predictions by smoothing out rapid fluctuations in weights during training.

Gradient checkpointing, a technique to reduce memory consumption during training, is facilitated by utilities in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/training/checkpoint.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/training/checkpoint.py). The [`create_custom_forward`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rf3/src/rf3/util_module.py#L33) function addresses a limitation in PyTorch's native [`checkpoint`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/docs/tutorials/RFdiffusion3_installation_tutorial.md#L258) function, allowing keyword arguments to be passed to checkpointed modules. This enables a wider range of neural network architectures to benefit from memory savings. The [`activation_checkpointing`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/training/checkpoint.py#L38) decorator provides a convenient way to apply this technique to a function's forward pass, conditionally wrapping it with gradient checkpointing only when gradients are enabled.

Learning rate control is managed through schedulers, particularly the [`AF3Scheduler`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/training/schedulers.py#L7) defined in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/training/schedulers.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/training/schedulers.py). This scheduler implements a two-phase learning rate schedule: an initial linear warmup phase where the learning rate gradually increases, followed by a decay phase where it decreases over time. This approach is common in deep learning to ensure stable convergence and prevent premature overfitting. Additionally, the [`SchedulerConfig`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/training/schedulers.py#L66) dataclass provides a standardized way to configure any learning rate scheduler, specifying how often it should be applied (per step or per epoch) and allowing for serialization and deserialization of its state.

### Advanced Utilities for Data, Model, and Distributed Management
Foundry's core library includes a comprehensive set of advanced utility modules designed to streamline complex machine learning workflows. These utilities manage data loading, model weight configurations, distributed training, and dynamic instantiation of components, ensuring efficient and scalable operations.

For sophisticated data management, Foundry provides tools for handling various data sources and structures. The [`SquashfsManager`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/squashfs.py#L18) in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/squashfs.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/squashfs.py) enables lazy mounting and caching of Squashfs filesystems, automatically cleaning them up upon program exit. This is particularly useful for managing large, immutable datasets efficiently. Alongside this, the module [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/datasets.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/datasets.py) offers robust capabilities for distributed loading and dataset composition, allowing for single, concatenated, or probability-mixed datasets, complete with fallback mechanisms and load balancing strategies for distributed environments.

Foundry also offers flexible mechanisms for managing model weights and applying parameter freezing policies. The module [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/weights.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/weights.py) defines [`WeightLoadingConfig`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/weights.py#L90) and [`ParameterFreezingConfig`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/weights.py#L119) to control how weights are loaded from checkpoints and which parameters should be frozen during training. These configurations support glob-pattern matching for fine-grained control, enabling policies such as re-initialization, zero-initialization, direct copying, or padded copying of weights.

Dynamic instantiation of callbacks and loggers is facilitated through the [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/instantiators.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/instantiators.py) module. This utility allows for the creation of [`BaseCallback`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py#L9) and [`Logger`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rf3/src/rf3/train.py#L36) objects directly from Hydra [`DictConfig`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/ddp.py#L7) instances, providing a flexible way to configure training workflows without hardcoding component types.

Distributed training is a key focus, with several utilities dedicated to setting up and managing multi-node and multi-GPU environments. The module [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/ddp.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/ddp.py) provides functions for determining the current process rank, checking for the rank-zero process, and automatically configuring the appropriate accelerator (e.g., CUDA, XPU, MPS, or CPU) based on hardware availability. This module also includes a [`RankedLogger`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/ddp.py#L58) for DDP-aware logging, which prefixes messages with the process rank and can be configured to log only from the rank-zero process. For systems equipped with Intel XPUs, Foundry offers specialized support through the [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/xpu`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/xpu) subdirectory. This includes [`XPUAccelerator`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/xpu/xpu_accelerator.py#L9) for managing XPU devices, [`SingleXPUStrategy`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/xpu/single_xpu_strategy.py#L13) for single-device training, and [`XPUMixedPrecision`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/xpu/xpu_precision.py#L11) for enabling automatic mixed precision specifically on XPU hardware. For a broader overview of training processes, refer to the [Training Harness and Distributed Training](#training-harness-and-distributed-training) section.

### Geometric and Tensor Operation Utilities
Utilities for geometric and tensor operations provide foundational capabilities for structural bioinformatics models, encompassing functions for aligning 3D point clouds, managing protein component identifiers, and performing rigid transformations.

For instance, the function [`weighted_rigid_align`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/alignment.py#L8) in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/alignment.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/alignment.py) performs a weighted rigid body alignment of a ground truth 3D point cloud onto another, crucial for comparing or superimposing molecular structures. This involves calculating centroids, forming a weighted covariance matrix, and using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to derive a rotation matrix that ensures a proper rotation without reflection. This module also includes [`get_rmsd`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/alignment.py#L87) for calculating Root Mean Square Deviation between point clouds.

The parsing and validation of protein or molecular component identifiers, often referred to as "contigs," are managed by functions within [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/components.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/components.py). These utilities convert contig strings (e.g., "A20-21" or "1-5") into structured representations, enabling the definition of fixed or variable regions in design patterns. Functions such as [`split_contig`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/components.py#L48), [`extract_pn_unit_info`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/components.py#L64), and [`get_design_pattern_with_constraints`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/components.py#L83) facilitate this conversion and validate input formats. Additionally, this module generates atom masks based on these identifiers using functions like [`get_name_mask`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/components.py#L254) and [`fetch_mask_from_idx`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/components.py#L352), which are essential for selecting specific parts of an [`AtomArray`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/examples/all.ipynb#L20).

Core utilities for 3D rigid transformations, including rotations and translations, are centralized in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rigid.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rigid.py). This module supports both rotation matrix and quaternion representations, providing low-level [`torch`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/README.md#L22) tensor operations for numerical stability and GPU acceleration. The [`Rotation`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rigid.py#L278) class encapsulates 3D rotations, offering methods for composition, inversion, and application to 3D points. Building upon this, the [`Rigid`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rigid.py#L850) class represents a full rigid transformation by combining a [`Rotation`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rigid.py#L278) object with a 3D translation vector. It provides analogous methods for composing transformations, applying them to points, and inverting them. The [`from_3_points`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rigid.py#L1249) static method is particularly notable for constructing a [`Rigid`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rigid.py#L850) transformation from three 3D points, a critical operation for defining local coordinate frames in structural biology.

Geometric augmentation, which involves applying random rotations and translations to batched atom coordinates, is handled by [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rotation_augmentation.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rotation_augmentation.py). Functions like [`centre_random_augmentation`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rotation_augmentation.py#L30) prepare input coordinates by centering them and then apply random transformations, such as [`uniform_random_rotation`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rotation_augmentation.py#L37), to introduce diversity in training data or design outputs.

Finally, general PyTorch utilities in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/torch.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/torch.py) support these geometric and tensor operations by providing functions for managing tensor device and data type transfers ([`map_to`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/torch.py#L27)), asserting tensor properties like shape and the absence of NaN values ([`assert_shape`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/torch.py#L154), [`_assert_no_nans`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/torch.py#L93)), and performing scatter-mean aggregations ([`scatter_mean`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/torch.py#L209)), ensuring robust and efficient tensor manipulation across the framework.

## Command Line Interface (CLI) Utilities
Foundry provides command-line interface (CLI) tools for managing model checkpoints, which are crucial for consistent and reproducible model usage. These utilities facilitate tasks such as installing new models, viewing available and installed checkpoints, and cleaning up storage. The core functionality for these operations resides within the [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry_cli`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry_cli) directory, with the primary logic implemented in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry_cli/download_checkpoints.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry_cli/download_checkpoints.py).

The CLI streamlines the process of obtaining and organizing pre-trained models. For example, users can install specific model checkpoints or an entire set of base models. The system determines where to store these checkpoints by resolving appropriate directories, which can be influenced by user-specified paths or environment variables. Downloads include integrity verification through SHA256 hashing to ensure files are not corrupted.

To aid in managing the downloaded assets, the CLI offers commands to list all models that are registered as available for download, along with their descriptions. It also allows users to inspect which models are currently installed on their system, providing information on their storage locations and cumulative size. For maintaining disk space, a cleanup command is available to remove all downloaded checkpoint files after user confirmation.

### Checkpoint Management: Installation and Resolution
The Foundry command-line interface (CLI) provides a mechanism for managing model checkpoints, particularly focusing on their installation and resolution. The [`install`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry_cli/download_checkpoints.py#L145) command in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry_cli/download_checkpoints.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry_cli/download_checkpoints.py) facilitates downloading and setting up model weights.

When a user executes the [`install`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry_cli/download_checkpoints.py#L145) command, the system first determines where these checkpoints should be stored. This involves a function, [`_resolve_checkpoint_dirs`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry_cli/download_checkpoints.py#L33) in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry_cli/download_checkpoints.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry_cli/download_checkpoints.py), which prioritizes any directory specified by the user. If no user-defined path is provided, it defaults to predefined locations. After identifying the primary storage directory, this path is recorded using [`append_checkpoint_to_env`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/inference_engines/checkpoint_registry.py#L49) to ensure consistency for future operations.

Once the target directory is established, the CLI proceeds to download the specified models. Each model download is handled by the [`install_model`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry_cli/download_checkpoints.py#L106) function in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry_cli/download_checkpoints.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry_cli/download_checkpoints.py). To ensure the integrity of the downloaded files, a SHA256 hash verification is performed, preventing the use of corrupted or altered model weights. This process allows users to easily obtain and integrate pre-trained models into their Foundry workflows.

### Checkpoint Management: Listing and Cleanup
The Foundry CLI provides utilities for managing model checkpoints, including commands to inspect available and installed models and to clean up downloaded files.

The [`list_available`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry_cli/download_checkpoints.py#L189) command in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry_cli/download_checkpoints.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry_cli/download_checkpoints.py) displays information about models that can be installed. This command queries a central registry of known models, [`REGISTERED_CHECKPOINTS`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/inference_engines/checkpoint_registry.py#L80), which contains metadata such as model names and descriptions. This allows users to see what models are supported and potentially download them.

For models already on the system, the [`list_installed`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry_cli/download_checkpoints.py#L197) command, also within [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry_cli/download_checkpoints.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry_cli/download_checkpoints.py), scans configured directories to identify and list [`.ckpt`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L832) and [`.pt`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry_cli/download_checkpoints.py#L205) files. It provides an overview of the checkpoints present, including their file names and total disk space consumed.

To free up storage, the [`clean`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry_cli/download_checkpoints.py#L226) command, located in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry_cli/download_checkpoints.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry_cli/download_checkpoints.py), facilitates the removal of all downloaded checkpoint files. Before deletion, it provides a summary of the files to be removed and their cumulative size, requiring user confirmation to prevent accidental data loss. This functionality helps maintain a tidy local environment by purging unnecessary model files.

## Machine Learning Callbacks
Foundry employs a standardized callback system to integrate various functionalities into its machine learning training workflows. This system allows for the dynamic injection of custom logic at different stages of the training and validation processes, promoting modularity and extensibility. The core of this system is the abstract [`BaseCallback`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py#L9) class, defined in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py), which provides a comprehensive set of hook methods that concrete implementations can override. These hooks allow interaction with the [`trainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/mpnn/src/mpnn/train.py#L287) object, providing access to its state and Fabric utilities.

Key functionalities implemented through this callback system include:

*   **Model Health Tracking**: The [`ActivationsGradientsWeightsTracker`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/health_logging.py#L48) callback in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/health_logging.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/health_logging.py) monitors and logs statistics of a model's gradients, weights, and activations. It registers hooks to capture activations and iterates over model parameters to collect summary statistics and histogram data. This tracking helps in diagnosing training issues and understanding model behavior over time.
*   **Validation Metrics Aggregation**: For distributed training, the [`StoreValidationMetricsInDFCallback`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/metrics_logging.py#L16) in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/metrics_logging.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/metrics_logging.py) collects and aggregates per-batch validation metrics across different processing ranks. It ensures that metrics generated on each rank are saved and then reliably combined by the global rank zero, handling potential duplicates to produce a unified view of validation performance.
*   **Performance Profiling**: The [`TimingCallback`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/timing_logging.py#L13) in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/timing_logging.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/timing_logging.py) provides detailed profiling of various training phases, such as data loading, forward and backward passes, and optimizer steps. It uses an internal [`Timers`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/torch.py#L330) object to measure durations, logging and optionally printing average timings at specified intervals to analyze and optimize training efficiency.
*   **Comprehensive Training Progress Logging**: Found in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/train_logging.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/train_logging.py), various callbacks are dedicated to logging training progress. These include callbacks for logging model parameter counts, debugging [`example_id`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/engine.py#L95)s per batch, monitoring dataset sampling ratios, tracking the optimizer's learning rate, and providing detailed breakdowns of training losses. These callbacks leverage rich console output for enhanced readability and structured reporting of key training metrics.

This callback architecture, as described further in [Training Harness with PyTorch Lightning Fabric](#foundry-core-library-and-ml-workflows-training-harness-with-pytorch-lightning-fabric), allows developers to inject custom logic for monitoring, logging, and dynamic adjustment of training parameters without altering the core training loop.

### Core Callback Design and Extension
The [`BaseCallback`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py#L9) class, defined in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py), establishes a standardized, extensible interface for injecting custom logic into the various stages of machine learning training and validation workflows. It is an abstract base class ([`ABC`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/logging.py#L200)), meaning it provides a blueprint for specific callback implementations to follow.

This foundational class defines numerous hook methods that correspond to distinct events within the training lifecycle. These hooks allow developers to execute code at precise moments, such as the start or end of the entire training run ([`on_fit_start`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py#L28), [`on_fit_end`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py#L32)), individual training epochs ([`on_train_epoch_start`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py#L37), [`on_train_epoch_end`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py#L81)), or validation epochs ([`on_validation_epoch_start`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py#L86), [`on_validation_epoch_end`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py#L113)).

Further granularity is provided by hooks that operate at the batch level. For instance, [`on_train_batch_start`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py#L49) and [`on_train_batch_end`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py#L53) allow logic to be run before and after the processing of each training batch. Similarly, [`on_validation_batch_start`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py#L90) and [`on_validation_batch_end`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py#L101) serve the same purpose during validation.

A critical set of hooks integrates with the optimization process. [`on_before_optimizer_step`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py#L59) is called just prior to the optimizer's weight update, while [`optimizer_step`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py#L75) is called immediately after. It is notable that [`optimizer_step`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py#L75) specifically provides access to the [`trainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/mpnn/src/mpnn/train.py#L287) object, which is crucial for interacting with the training environment post-optimization.

Most of these hook methods receive a [`trainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/mpnn/src/mpnn/train.py#L287) object, providing access to the overall training state, configuration, and underlying PyTorch Lightning Fabric functionalities (accessible via [`trainer.fabric`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rf3/src/rf3/train.py#L110)). This design promotes modularity, enabling developers to implement custom behaviors for tasks like logging, monitoring, early stopping, or dynamic adjustment of training parameters without altering the core training loop. For examples of concrete implementations and their applications, refer to [Model Health Tracking and Visualization](#machine-learning-callbacks-model-health-tracking-and-visualization), [Distributed Validation Metrics Aggregation](#machine-learning-callbacks-distributed-validation-metrics-aggregation), [Training Phase Timing and Performance Profiling](#machine-learning-callbacks-training-phase-timing-and-performance-profiling), and [Comprehensive Training Progress Logging and Loss Monitoring](#machine-learning-callbacks-comprehensive-training-progress-logging-and-loss-monitoring).

### Model Health Tracking and Visualization
Foundry employs the [`ActivationsGradientsWeightsTracker`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/health_logging.py#L48) callback, defined in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/health_logging.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/health_logging.py), to monitor the health of neural network models during training. This callback is a specialized implementation of the [Core Callback Design and Extension](#machine-learning-callbacks-core-callback-design-and-extension) and tracks key statistics related to a model's activations, gradients, and weights. It is particularly useful for identifying issues such as vanishing or exploding gradients, or dead neurons, which can impede model training.

The [`ActivationsGradientsWeightsTracker`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/health_logging.py#L48) operates by integrating into the training loop, utilizing various hooks to collect data. During training batches, it registers forward hooks on specified modules to capture activation data. Before each optimizer step, it gathers statistics from model parameters, including gradients and weights. This information can be collected as scalar metrics (e.g., mean, standard deviation, norm, min, max) or as histogram data, providing a detailed view of the distributions. The callback offers flexible filtering mechanisms, allowing users to specify which parameters or modules to track, reducing computational overhead and focusing on relevant components. All logging operations are designed to function correctly within distributed training environments by ensuring metrics are collected and reported only by the main process. Additionally, the module provides utility functions, [`plot_tensor_hist`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/health_logging.py#L258) and [`plot_tensor_stats`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/health_logging.py#L324), for visualizing the collected time-series and histogram data, enabling a quick assessment of how these critical health indicators evolve over the training process.

### Distributed Validation Metrics Aggregation
The [`StoreValidationMetricsInDFCallback`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/metrics_logging.py#L16) class in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/metrics_logging.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/metrics_logging.py) facilitates the collection and aggregation of validation metrics, particularly in distributed training environments. Its primary function is to gather per-batch validation outputs from each processing rank into a dedicated DataFrame.

During validation, the callback accumulates metrics for each batch into a pandas [`DataFrame`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/logging.py#L176) ([`per_gpu_outputs_df`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/metrics_logging.py#L34)) specific to each GPU or rank. At the close of each validation epoch, every rank saves its accumulated DataFrame to a temporary CSV file. Following this, a synchronization barrier ensures all processes have completed saving. Subsequently, the global rank zero aggregates these temporary CSVs, merging them into a single DataFrame. This aggregation process includes logic to handle potential duplicate entries by tracking unique [`example_id`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/engine.py#L95) and [`dataset`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/README.md#L106) combinations, ensuring each distinct example is recorded only once. Finally, rank zero is responsible for cleaning up all temporary CSV files. The [`metrics_to_save`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/mpnn/src/mpnn/train.py#L283) parameter offers flexibility, allowing users to specify a subset of metrics for storage, thereby managing the size of the DataFrame.

### Training Phase Timing and Performance Profiling
The [`TimingCallback`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/timing_logging.py#L13) within Foundry's training framework provides performance profiling for various training phases, such as data loading iteration, the overall training step, and the optimizer step. This callback, found in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/timing_logging.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/timing_logging.py), utilizes a [`Timers`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/torch.py#L330) object to measure durations.

The callback integrates with the training lifecycle through several hooks. It uses [`on_train_epoch_start`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py#L37) and [`on_after_train_loader_iter`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py#L41) to measure the duration of data loader iterations. The [`train_step`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/timing_logging.py#L41) and [`forward_loss_backward`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/timing_logging.py#L45) durations are tracked using [`on_before_train_loader_next`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py#L45), [`on_train_batch_start`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py#L49), and [`on_train_batch_end`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py#L53). The [`optimizer_step`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py#L75) duration is measured by [`on_before_optimizer_step`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py#L59) and [`on_after_optimizer_step`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py#L65).

After each optimizer step, [`TimingCallback`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/timing_logging.py#L13) accumulates these durations. It then logs and, if enabled, prints the average timings over a configurable number of steps. This aggregation provides a stable overview of performance characteristics without overwhelming the logs with per-step details. All logging and timing operations are executed only on the global rank zero process in distributed environments, leveraging the [`@rank_zero_only`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/logging.py#L126) decorator to prevent redundant outputs. For more details on the general callback system, refer to [Callback System for Training Workflow Automation](#foundry-core-library-and-ml-workflows-callback-system-for-training-workflow-automation) and [Core Callback Design and Extension](#machine-learning-callbacks-core-callback-design-and-extension).

### Comprehensive Training Progress Logging and Loss Monitoring
This section discusses the various callbacks that facilitate monitoring and reporting of key training metrics, loss breakdowns, and resource usage with structured console output. These callbacks are located in the [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/train_logging.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/train_logging.py) file.

The [`LogModelParametersCallback`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/train_logging.py#L26) records the total and trainable parameters of a model when training commences, providing a snapshot of the model's complexity. For debugging purposes, the [`PrintExampleIDBeforeForwardPassCallback`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/train_logging.py#L33) can be used to output the unique identifier of each example processed in a batch, along with its rank, epoch, and batch information.

To understand dataset utilization, the [`LogDatasetSamplingRatiosCallback`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/train_logging.py#L58) monitors and logs the proportions of data sampled from different datasets during an epoch. This is achieved by tracking [`example_id`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/engine.py#L95) information from incoming batches and summarizing the distribution at the end of each training epoch.

The [`LogLearningRateCallback`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/train_logging.py#L93) tracks the learning rate of the optimizer, reporting its value at regular intervals throughout training. This allows monitoring of learning rate schedules and adjustments over time.

For a detailed view of training performance, the [`LogAF3TrainingLossesCallback`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/train_logging.py#L116) provides comprehensive logging of various loss components. It tracks individual loss types using [`MeanMetric`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/train_logging.py#L14) instances, records the start time of each epoch, and processes the outputs of each training batch to update these metrics. At specified intervals, it logs mean batch losses and can optionally log per-structure losses. At the end of each epoch, it summarizes the average losses, total optimizer steps, number of batches processed, and overall epoch duration. This callback leverages the [`rich`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/pyproject.toml#L31) library for enhanced console output, presenting information in structured panels and tables, improving readability and aiding in quick assessment of training progress.

## Inference Engines and Model Execution
The [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/inference_engines`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/inference_engines) directory forms the foundation for managing model setup, configuration, and checkpoint loading for inference within the Foundry ecosystem. This framework simplifies the complexities of model instantiation and execution, providing a consistent interface for various biomolecular design models.

The [`BaseInferenceEngine`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/inference_engines/base.py#L33) class, located in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/inference_engines/base.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/inference_engines/base.py), serves as the core abstraction. It handles tasks such as resolving and loading model checkpoints, applying configuration overrides using tools like Hydra and OmegaConf, and setting up the model's data transformation pipeline and trainer components. This design ensures that resource-intensive setup operations are performed efficiently, separate from the actual inference runs. The engine supports flexible configuration merging, allowing for dynamic adjustments to model behavior and inference parameters. Additionally, it provides built-in support for distributed inference setups, leveraging parameters like [`num_nodes`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/engine.py#L78) and [`devices_per_node`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/engine.py#L79).

A crucial aspect of the inference engine is its robust checkpoint management system, detailed in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/inference_engines/checkpoint_registry.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/inference_engines/checkpoint_registry.py). This system resolves checkpoint file paths by prioritizing environment variables ([`FOUNDRY_CHECKPOINT_DIRS`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/.env#L63)), falling back to a default user directory, and includes mechanisms for persisting these configurations in [`.env`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/.env#L2) files.
