The [`RegisteredCheckpoint`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/inference_engines/checkpoint_registry.py#L65) dataclass and the [`REGISTERED_CHECKPOINTS`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/inference_engines/checkpoint_registry.py#L80) dictionary provide a centralized registry for known model checkpoints, simplifying their identification and location. This allows users to reference common models by mnemonic names, streamlining the workflow for loading and executing inference with established Foundry models.

### BaseInferenceEngine Architecture and Configuration
The [`BaseInferenceEngine`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/inference_engines/base.py#L33) class, located in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/inference_engines/base.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/inference_engines/base.py), establishes a foundational architecture for managing and executing inference workflows for machine learning models. This design separates the complex process of model setup and configuration from the actual execution of inference runs, allowing for efficient and repeatable operations.

During initialization, the [`BaseInferenceEngine`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/inference_engines/base.py#L33) handles various setup tasks, including configuring logging, resolving paths to model checkpoints, and applying user-defined configuration overrides. It supports referencing predefined models through a checkpoint registry, which maps mnemonic keys to metadata, simplifying model identification and location. See [Checkpoint Registry and Path Resolution](#inference-engines-and-model-execution-checkpoint-registry-and-path-resolution) for more information on how checkpoints are managed. The engine uses a seed management system to ensure reproducibility.

The core of the [`BaseInferenceEngine`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/inference_engines/base.py#L33)'s configuration management relies on [`hydra`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/pyproject.toml#L27) and [`omegaconf`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/ddp.py#L7). These libraries facilitate dynamic instantiation of model components and flexible merging of configuration settings. This allows the system to load a model's training configuration from a checkpoint and then dynamically apply overrides for inference-specific parameters, such as transformations or inference sampler settings. The [`initialize`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/engine.py#L219) method is responsible for loading the model and its configuration, merging any provided overrides with the checkpoint's training configuration, and then constructing the data transformation pipeline and the trainer component. This method is designed to be idempotent, ensuring that these resource-intensive setup steps are executed only once.

The [`BaseInferenceEngine`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/inference_engines/base.py#L33) also supports context management, allowing it to be used within [`with`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/README.md#L1) statements. This ensures proper cleanup and release of resources associated with the trainer and data pipeline components once inference tasks are completed. The actual logic for performing inference is abstract and must be implemented by subclasses, which define how the model processes inputs and generates outputs for specific applications.

### Checkpoint Registry and Path Resolution
Checkpoint management within Foundry addresses the need to locate, verify, and register pre-trained models. The system prioritizes flexibility by allowing checkpoint paths to be resolved from multiple sources, including environment variables and user-defined directories. This ensures that models can be easily accessed regardless of their storage location.

The primary mechanism for locating checkpoints involves functions that gather potential directory paths. These functions consider environment variables such as [`FOUNDRY_CHECKPOINT_DIRS`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/.env#L63) and [`FOUNDRY_CHECKPOINTS_DIR`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/inference_engines/checkpoint_registry.py#L34), along with a default user directory, to establish a comprehensive search order. The [`append_checkpoint_to_env`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/inference_engines/checkpoint_registry.py#L49) utility facilitates persistence by allowing these configured directories to be saved to [`.env`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/.env#L2) files, streamlining future access.

To simplify the use of known models, Foundry employs a registry system. The [`RegisteredCheckpoint`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/inference_engines/checkpoint_registry.py#L65) dataclass, defined in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/inference_engines/checkpoint_registry.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/inference_engines/checkpoint_registry.py), stores essential metadata for each checkpoint, including its download URL, expected filename, a descriptive text, and an optional SHA256 checksum for integrity verification. A global dictionary, [`REGISTERED_CHECKPOINTS`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/inference_engines/checkpoint_registry.py#L80), maps mnemonic identifiers (e.g., "rfd3na", "proteinmpnn") to these [`RegisteredCheckpoint`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/inference_engines/checkpoint_registry.py#L65) instances. This registry acts as a central catalog, enabling inference engines and other components to refer to specific models by name rather than requiring a direct file path. When a registered checkpoint is requested, its [`get_default_path`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/inference_engines/checkpoint_registry.py#L71) method attempts to locate the actual file within the established search paths, providing the path to the first existing match or suggesting a default download location if not found. This integration simplifies model loading and ensures consistency across different inference tasks. See [BaseInferenceEngine Architecture and Configuration](#inference-engines-and-model-execution-baseinferenceengine-architecture-and-configuration) for how these checkpoints are utilized by the inference engine.

## Model Evaluation Metrics and Loss Functions
The Foundry framework provides a structured approach for evaluating machine learning models through a standardized system for metrics and loss functions. This system is designed to streamline the assessment of model performance and the aggregation of various loss components during training.

The foundation of this system is the [`Metric`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L184) abstract base class, defined in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py). This class serves as a blueprint for all custom evaluation metrics. Developers extend this class and implement a [`compute`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L319) method to define their specific metric calculations. The [`Metric`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L184) class also includes mechanisms for handling input arguments, allowing metrics to specify how data from a larger input dictionary should be mapped to the arguments of their [`compute`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L319) method. This includes identifying both required and optional arguments. Furthermore, metrics can be conditionally computed based on tags, enabling flexible evaluation scenarios where certain metrics are only relevant under specific conditions.

To manage and execute these individual metrics, Foundry utilizes the [`MetricManager`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L40) class, also found in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py). The [`MetricManager`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L40) is responsible for orchestrating the instantiation, filtering, and execution of multiple [`Metric`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L184) instances. When invoked, it processes input data, applies any tag-based filtering defined on the metrics, and then calls the [`compute_from_kwargs`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L249) method for each relevant metric. The results from these computations are then aggregated into a single dictionary, with clear naming conventions (e.g., prefixing keys with the metric's name) to distinguish results from different metrics. The [`MetricManager`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L40) also incorporates error handling, allowing for either the raising or suppression of exceptions that occur during metric computation.

For training, Foundry includes a [`Loss`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/losses.py#L8) class, located in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/losses.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/losses.py), which facilitates the aggregation of multiple individual loss functions into a single composite loss. This class dynamically instantiates [`torch.nn.Module`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/mpnn/src/mpnn/utils/weights.py#L20) based loss functions from a configuration. During the forward pass, the [`Loss`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/losses.py#L8) class computes each registered loss function, sums their scalar values to produce a [`total_loss`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/losses.py#L35), and collects detailed metrics from each into a comprehensive loss dictionary. This approach provides a unified training objective while still allowing for granular insights into the contributions of individual loss components.

### Metric Definition and Customization
The Foundry framework provides an abstract base class, [`Metric`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L184), found in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py), which serves as the foundation for defining custom evaluation metrics. Developers extend this class to implement specific calculations by overriding the [`compute`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L319) method. This method is designed to accept arbitrary keyword arguments and is expected to return a dictionary or a list of dictionaries containing the calculated metric values.

To manage how input data maps to the [`compute`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L319) method's arguments, [`Metric`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L184) offers properties like [`kwargs_to_compute_args`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L284) and [`optional_kwargs`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L303). [`kwargs_to_compute_args`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L284) allows for custom mapping of incoming keyword arguments to those expected by [`compute`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L319), enabling flexible data extraction from complex input structures. [`optional_kwargs`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L303) specifies arguments that are not strictly required, preventing errors if they are absent from the input. Conversely, [`required_compute_args`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L237) and [`required_kwargs`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L242) help identify the essential arguments needed for metric calculation.

Metrics can also be configured for conditional computation based on [`tags`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L188) provided in an [`extra_info`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L46) dictionary. This enables metrics to be activated or deactivated depending on specific conditions or properties of the data being evaluated, using [`required_tags_all`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L151), [`required_tags_any`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L155), and [`prohibited_tags`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L159). The [`compute_from_kwargs`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L249) method acts as an intermediary, processing the raw input to prepare the correct arguments for the [`compute`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L319) method, ensuring that metrics receive their necessary data in the expected format.

The [`Metric`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L184) class, along with [`MetricManager`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L40) and [`MetricInputError`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L36), is made publicly available through [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/__init__.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/__init__.py). For a broader understanding of how these metrics are orchestrated and executed, see [MetricManager for Orchestration and Execution](#model-evaluation-metrics-and-loss-functions-metricmanager-for-orchestration-and-execution).

### MetricManager for Orchestration and Execution
The [`MetricManager`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L40) class, defined in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py), is central to orchestrating the evaluation of machine learning models within Foundry. It streamlines the process of managing, filtering, and executing multiple [`Metric`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L184) instances, which are abstract representations of individual evaluation criteria. The manager is responsible for instantiating these metrics from configuration, applying conditional filtering based on tags, executing their computation methods, and aggregating their results into a unified output.

When invoked, the [`MetricManager`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L40) iterates through its collection of [`Metric`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L184) objects. For each metric, it first determines if it should be computed based on a tag-based filtering mechanism, which uses [`metrics_tags`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L148) provided in the input [`extra_info`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L46) dictionary. This allows for selective metric computation relevant to specific conditions or data subsets. If a metric is eligible, the manager calls its [`compute_from_kwargs`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L249) method, which intelligently maps the available input data to the arguments expected by the individual metric's computation logic.

The results from each successfully computed metric are then aggregated. If a metric returns a dictionary, its keys are prefixed with the metric's name to ensure uniqueness and clarity in the final output (e.g., [`my_metric.value`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L60)). If a list is returned, it is stored directly under the metric's name. The manager also includes an [`example_id`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/engine.py#L95) in the final results dictionary for traceability. Error reporting during metric computation is handled using [`error.context`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L164) for structured logging, and the [`raise_errors`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L58) flag at initialization determines whether computation failures lead to exceptions or are gracefully suppressed. The [`MetricInputError`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/metric.py#L36) is a specific exception raised when there are issues with the input data provided to a metric. For more details on defining individual metrics, refer to [Metric Definition and Customization](#model-evaluation-metrics-and-loss-functions-metric-definition-and-customization).

### Loss Function Aggregation with the Loss Class
The [`Loss`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/losses.py#L8) class, defined in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/losses.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/losses.py), provides a mechanism for aggregating multiple individual loss functions into a single composite loss. This is particularly useful in machine learning models where various aspects of the model's output or different data modalities contribute to the overall training objective.

Upon instantiation, the [`Loss`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/losses.py#L8) class dynamically loads and initializes individual loss functions. These individual losses are expected to be instances of [`torch.nn.Module`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/mpnn/src/mpnn/utils/weights.py#L20), enabling diverse loss types to be combined. This dynamic instantiation leverages Hydra, allowing for flexible configuration of the specific loss functions and their parameters.

During a forward pass, the [`Loss`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/losses.py#L8) class iterates through each registered individual loss function, computing its contribution based on the network's input and output. The scalar values from these individual losses are summed to produce a [`total_loss`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/metrics/losses.py#L35). Concurrently, detailed metrics from each individual loss function are collected and stored in a dictionary, providing granular insights into the performance of each component of the overall loss. This approach simplifies the management of complex loss landscapes, ensuring that all relevant training signals are appropriately combined and tracked.

## Neural Network Building Blocks
Foundry provides foundational neural network components within the [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/model`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/model) directory that serve as building blocks for more complex models. These components include specialized layers for handling scalar inputs and implementing flexible dropout mechanisms.

One such component is the [`FourierEmbedding`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/model/layers/blocks.py#L7) class, located in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/model/layers/blocks.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/model/layers/blocks.py). This class is designed to encode scalar inputs into a higher-dimensional feature space using Fourier features. This transformation helps models capture periodic patterns and improve their ability to learn complex relationships from simple scalar inputs by providing a richer representation.

Another key building block is the [`Dropout`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/model/layers/blocks.py#L32) class, also found in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/model/layers/blocks.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/model/layers/blocks.py). This implementation of dropout offers a broadcastable mechanism, allowing the system to drop entire rows or columns of a tensor, rather than individual elements. This flexibility is particularly useful for applying dropout consistently across specific dimensions of a data representation, contributing to model regularization and preventing overfitting during training.

### Fourier Feature Encoding with `FourierEmbedding`
The [`FourierEmbedding`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/model/layers/blocks.py#L7) class, found in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/model/layers/blocks.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/model/layers/blocks.py), implements a Fourier feature encoding technique for scalar inputs. This method transforms a single scalar value into a higher-dimensional representation using cosine functions. This expansion allows neural networks to better capture periodic patterns and fine-grained details within the input data, which can be particularly useful for tasks involving spatial or temporal coordinates.

The class includes a [`reset_parameters`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/model/layers/blocks.py#L20) method for initializing the learnable weight ([`w`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/model/layers/blocks.py#L10)) and bias ([`b`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/model/layers/blocks.py#L11)) parameters that define the mapping. During its forward pass, [`FourierEmbedding`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/model/layers/blocks.py#L7) computes [`torch.cos(2 * pi * (t[..., None] * self.w + self.b))`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/model/layers/blocks.py#L4), where [`t`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/Makefile#L52) is the input scalar. This mathematical operation effectively projects the scalar into a feature space where its position can be uniquely and periodically encoded, thereby enriching the input representation for subsequent neural network layers.

### Broadcastable Dropout with `Dropout`
The [`Dropout`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/model/layers/blocks.py#L32) class, defined in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/model/layers/blocks.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/model/layers/blocks.py), implements a flexible broadcastable dropout mechanism. This allows for dropout to be applied not just to individual elements, but to entire rows or columns of a tensor, depending on the [`broadcast_dim`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/model/layers/blocks.py#L34) parameter. The [`p_drop`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/model/layers/blocks.py#L34) parameter controls the probability of an element being dropped. During training, [`Dropout`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/model/layers/blocks.py#L32) uses a [`torch.distributions.bernoulli.Bernoulli`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/model/layers/blocks.py#L37) distribution to sample a binary mask, which is then applied to the input tensor. This masked input is scaled to maintain the expected sum. During evaluation, the [`Dropout`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/model/layers/blocks.py#L32) layer passes the input through without modification, ensuring consistent output for inference. This functionality is part of the broader collection of [Neural Network Building Blocks](#neural-network-building-blocks) available in Foundry.

## Training Harness and Distributed Training
Foundry utilizes a generic training harness, implemented as the [`FabricTrainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L56) class found in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py), built upon PyTorch Lightning Fabric. This harness orchestrates the entire lifecycle of model training, including setup, configuration, validation, and checkpointing, with inherent support for distributed training environments. It integrates features such as Exponential Moving Average (EMA) for model smoothing and improved generalization, and provides support for Intel XPU accelerators, ensuring scalable and efficient model development.

The [`FabricTrainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L56) manages the initialization and configuration of the training environment, defining parameters such as the accelerator type, distributed strategy, and precision. It maintains a central state that tracks heterogeneous training components like the model, optimizer, scheduler configuration, global step count, and current epoch. This allows for flexible and dynamic construction of models, optimizers, and learning rate schedulers, often leveraging Hydra for configuration, and can wrap models with EMA if specified.

During the training process, the [`FabricTrainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L56) orchestrates the main training loop, which includes iterating through epochs, managing gradient accumulation, and executing the forward and backward passes. It also handles the logic for stepping the optimizer, applying gradient clipping, and updating the learning rate scheduler based on configurable levels and frequencies. For robust training, it incorporates mechanisms to check for and skip NaN/Inf gradients.

A key aspect of the [`FabricTrainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L56) is its comprehensive checkpointing system. It allows for saving and loading the complete state of the trainer, including the model, optimizer, and scheduler states. This intelligent restoration capability supports policy-based weight loading and parameter freezing, ensuring continuity and flexibility in training experiments. The system can also identify the latest checkpoint within a specified directory, streamlining the resumption of training.

### FabricTrainer: Core Architecture and Lifecycle Management
The [`FabricTrainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L56) found in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py) is an abstract base class that orchestrates the entire lifecycle of a deep learning model's training process. It leverages PyTorch Lightning Fabric to manage various aspects of training, from initial setup to the iterative training and validation loops, and finally to checkpointing and state restoration.

Upon instantiation, the [`FabricTrainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L56) configures the [`L.Fabric`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L163) instance, which is central to handling distributed training, mixed precision, and accelerator (e.g., GPU, XPU) setups. This configuration includes parameters such as the accelerator type, strategy for distributed training, number of devices per node, and precision settings, as well as integrating callbacks and loggers. The trainer maintains a comprehensive internal [`state`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L60) dictionary, which stores essential training components like the model, optimizer, scheduler configuration, global step count, current epoch, and training configuration. This state can be initialized or updated, allowing for flexible management of the training process.

The main [`fit`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L329) method serves as the entry point for training, coordinating the overall flow. It sets up dataloaders, optionally loads a pre-existing checkpoint, performs an initial validation run, and then iterates through epochs. During each epoch, it executes dedicated [`train_loop`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L510) and [`validation_loop`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L598) methods. The [`train_loop`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L510) is responsible for processing training batches, accumulating gradients over several steps, and performing optimizer and scheduler updates. Conversely, the [`validation_loop`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L598) evaluates the model on the validation dataset. The [`FabricTrainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L56) also incorporates robust checkpointing mechanisms, allowing it to save its complete state (model weights, optimizer state, scheduler state, epoch, and global step) and intelligently restore it. This enables seamless resumption of training and facilitates advanced scenarios like applying specific weight loading policies or resetting optimizer states upon loading.

### Component Construction and Setup
The [`FabricTrainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L56) orchestrates the dynamic instantiation and preparation of critical training components: models, optimizers, and learning rate schedulers. Configuration for these components is typically handled using Hydra, allowing for flexible and declarative definitions. Once constructed, these components are prepared for PyTorch Lightning Fabric's distributed environment. A key feature is the optional wrapping of models with an Exponential Moving Average (EMA), which can enhance model stability and generalization during training. This component construction and setup process is foundational to the overall training lifecycle managed by the [Training Harness with PyTorch Lightning Fabric](#foundry-core-library-and-ml-workflows-training-harness-with-pytorch-lightning-fabric).

### Training and Validation Loop Mechanics
The [`FabricTrainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L56) orchestrates the complete training lifecycle, with [`fit`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L329) serving as the primary entry point. This method sets up dataloaders, manages checkpoint loading, performs an initial validation if configured, and iterates through epochs, checking for conditions to stop early.

Within each epoch, the [`train_loop`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L510) is responsible for processing training batches. It incorporates features like gradient accumulation, where gradients are computed over multiple batches before a single optimizer step, allowing for larger effective batch sizes without increased memory consumption. The [`train_loop`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L510) calls the abstract [`training_step`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L661) method for each batch, which must be implemented by concrete trainers to define the model's forward and backward passes. Following the [`training_step`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L661), the [`step_optimizer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L730) method performs the weight updates, including handling NaN/Inf gradient checks and optional gradient clipping. If an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) is configured for the model, [`step_optimizer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L730) also manages its updates. Concurrently, the [`step_scheduler`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L787) updates the learning rate based on the defined schedule.

The [`validation_loop`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L598) executes periodically to assess model performance on a validation dataset. During this loop, the model is set to evaluation mode to disable operations like dropout, and it iterates through validation batches. For each batch, the abstract [`validation_step`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L681) method is invoked, which, similar to [`training_step`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L661), must be implemented by subclasses to perform the forward pass and compute validation metrics. After the validation loop, the model reverts to training mode. Both [`training_step`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L661) and [`validation_step`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L681) are defined as abstract methods in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py), requiring specific implementations by any trainer extending [`FabricTrainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L56).

For a deeper understanding of the trainer's architecture, including how components are constructed and managed, refer to [FabricTrainer: Core Architecture and Lifecycle Management](#training-harness-and-distributed-training-fabrictrainer-core-architecture-and-lifecycle-management) and [Component Construction and Setup](#training-harness-and-distributed-training-component-construction-and-setup). The overall design of the [`FabricTrainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L56) is discussed in [Training Harness with PyTorch Lightning Fabric](#foundry-core-library-and-ml-workflows-training-harness-with-pytorch-lightning-fabric).

### Checkpointing and State Restoration
The training process within Foundry includes a robust checkpointing system, managed primarily by the [`FabricTrainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L56) defined in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py). This system ensures the ability to save and restore the complete state of a training run, which is crucial for resuming interrupted training, evaluating models at different stages, or transferring learned weights.

The [`FabricTrainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L56)'s [`save_checkpoint`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L815) method captures the current [`state`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L60) of the trainer. This state typically includes the model's parameters, the optimizer's state, the learning rate scheduler's state, the current training epoch, and the global step. This comprehensive saving ensures that a training run can be precisely re-established from a checkpoint.

Conversely, the [`load_checkpoint`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L868) method handles the intelligent restoration of this state. It can load a checkpoint from a specified path or a dictionary, meticulously restoring the model, optimizer, and scheduler to their states at the time the checkpoint was saved. This method also integrates with configurations such as [`weight_loading_config`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/weights.py#L273) and [`reset_optimizer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/weights.py#L272). The [`weight_loading_config`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/weights.py#L273) allows for policy-based loading of model weights, enabling scenarios like re-initializing specific layers, copying weights with padding, or freezing certain parameters. The [`reset_optimizer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/weights.py#L272) flag offers control over whether the optimizer's state should also be reset, which can be useful when fine-tuning a model or debugging. Furthermore, the system includes a static utility method, [`get_latest_checkpoint`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L931), to automatically locate the most recent checkpoint file within a given directory, streamlining the resumption of training.

## General Utilities for Deep Learning Infrastructure
Foundry's deep learning infrastructure relies on a collection of general utility functions to manage data, model weights, distributed training, and geometric operations. These utilities streamline common tasks in machine learning workflows, providing a standardized approach to handling various aspects of model development and deployment.

For data management, the system includes capabilities for handling Squashfs filesystems and organizing datasets. The [`SquashfsManager`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/squashfs.py#L18) in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/squashfs.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/squashfs.py) offers lazy mounting and caching of Squashfs filesystems, ensuring that data is accessed efficiently and unmounted properly upon program exit. This is particularly useful for managing large, read-only datasets. Complementing this, utilities in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/datasets.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/datasets.py) provide mechanisms for instantiating and composing datasets, supporting both single and combined datasets, with options for distributed loading and fallback strategies to enhance robustness.

Model weight management is handled through utilities in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/weights.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/weights.py), which facilitate loading model weights from checkpoints and applying parameter freezing policies. These policies allow for selective reinitialization, zero initialization, or copying of weights based on glob patterns, offering fine-grained control over model parameters during transfer learning or fine-tuning. Dynamic instantiation of callbacks and loggers is managed by functions in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/instantiators.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/instantiators.py), which leverage Hydra for creating [`BaseCallback`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py#L9) and [`Logger`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rf3/src/rf3/train.py#L36) objects from configuration, making the training pipeline highly configurable. For further details on callbacks, see [Machine Learning Callbacks](#machine-learning-callbacks).

Distributed training setups are supported by utilities in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/ddp.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/ddp.py), which assist in determining the current process rank and configuring accelerators based on hardware availability. This ensures that training jobs can scale efficiently across multiple GPUs or CPUs. Logging in these distributed environments is handled by a ranked logger that can filter messages to report only from the main process, reducing log clutter. More extensive logging capabilities, including warning suppression and structured configuration printing, are provided in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/logging.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/logging.py).

Geometric operations, crucial for structural bioinformatics models, are addressed through utilities that manage rigid body transformations and geometric augmentation. The [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rigid.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rigid.py) module provides fundamental operations for 3D rotations and translations, encapsulating them in [`Rotation`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rigid.py#L278) and [`Rigid`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rigid.py#L850) classes. These classes support various representations (e.g., rotation matrices, quaternions) and operations like composition, inversion, and application to 3D points. Building upon this, [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rotation_augmentation.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rotation_augmentation.py) offers methods for applying random rotations and translations to batched atom coordinates, which helps improve model generalization by introducing variability in training data. Utilities in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/alignment.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/alignment.py) are used for aligning 3D point clouds and calculating RMSD, important for comparing structural predictions. Additionally, [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/components.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/components.py) handles parsing and validating protein component identifiers (contigs) to generate atom masks, facilitating the selection and manipulation of specific molecular regions.

### Data Management and Squashfs Filesystems
Foundry's data management capabilities address the complexities of handling diverse datasets, particularly in distributed machine learning environments, and efficiently manage large, immutable data archives. A key aspect is the [`SquashfsManager`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/squashfs.py#L18), implemented in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/squashfs.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/squashfs.py), which provides a singleton pattern for lazy mounting and caching of Squashfs filesystems. This manager automatically handles the mounting of [`.sqfs`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/squashfs.py#L51) files on demand, caches their mount points for performance, and ensures their proper unmounting when the program exits, even in multiprocessing scenarios. This abstraction prevents resource leaks and simplifies data access from these compressed, read-only archives.

Complementing this, the [`assemble_distributed_loader`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/datasets.py#L230) function within [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/datasets.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/datasets.py) offers robust mechanisms for dataset instantiation, composition, and distributed loading. It supports various dataset structures, including single datasets, concatenated datasets (composed of multiple datasets joined sequentially), and probability-mixed datasets (where examples are sampled from different sub-datasets according to specified probabilities). The module integrates with Hydra for flexible configuration of datasets and samplers, allowing dynamic creation of these components. For distributed training, it assembles PyTorch [`DataLoader`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/mpnn/src/mpnn/train.py#L16) instances with appropriate distributed samplers, converting standard samplers into their distributed counterparts (e.g., [`MixedSampler`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/datasets.py#L8) to [`DistributedMixedSampler`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/mpnn/src/mpnn/train.py#L12), [`RandomSampler`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/datasets.py#L15) to [`DistributedSampler`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/datasets.py#L21)). It also includes [`wrap_dataset_and_sampler_with_fallbacks`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/datasets.py#L43) to provide a retry mechanism for data fetching, enhancing resilience against transient data loading errors. This system ensures efficient and reliable data provisioning across multiple training processes.

### Model Weight Management and Parameter Freezing
Foundry provides a system for managing model weights and applying parameter freezing policies, crucial for tasks such as fine-tuning or transfer learning. This system allows for flexible control over how weights are loaded from a checkpoint into a model and which parameters are subsequently frozen during training.

At the core of this system is the concept of a [`WeightLoadingPolicy`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/weights.py#L23), which defines strategies for handling individual parameters. These policies include [`REINIT`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/weights.py#L27) (retaining the model's default initialization), [`ZERO_INIT`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/weights.py#L30) (initializing parameters with zeros), [`COPY`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/weights.py#L33) (copying weights only if their shapes precisely match), and [`COPY_AND_ZERO_PAD`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/weights.py#L36) (copying existing data and padding with zeros if shapes differ but ranks match). These policies can be configured globally or for specific parameters using glob-style pattern matching, enabling fine-grained control over the weight loading process.

The [`WeightLoadingConfig`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/weights.py#L90) is a dataclass used to define these policies, specifying a default policy, a fallback policy, and a dictionary mapping parameter names or patterns to particular policies. Similarly, the [`ParameterFreezingConfig`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/weights.py#L119) allows for freezing specific parameters by setting their [`requires_grad`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rigid.py#L499) attribute to [`False`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/examples/all.ipynb#L177), supporting both default freezing behavior and pattern-based exceptions.

The [`load_weights_with_policies`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/weights.py#L164) function in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/weights.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/weights.py) orchestrates the application of these policies. It iterates through a model's parameters and, based on the [`WeightLoadingConfig`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/weights.py#L90), applies the appropriate policy to each. This function is designed to handle potential inconsistencies between the model's architecture and the loaded checkpoint by attempting a fallback policy if the primary one fails. After weights are loaded, the [`freeze_parameters_with_config`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/weights.py#L146) function uses the [`ParameterFreezingConfig`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/weights.py#L119) to set the [`requires_grad`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rigid.py#L499) attribute for chosen parameters, effectively freezing them.

This modular approach ensures that model developers can precisely control how pre-trained weights are integrated and adapted for new tasks, optimizing for memory, training efficiency, and model performance. Further details on how these configurations are managed during training can be found in [Training Utilities: EMA, Checkpointing, and Schedulers](#foundry-core-library-and-ml-workflows-training-utilities-ema-checkpointing-and-schedulers).

### Dynamic Instantiation of Callbacks and Loggers
Foundry uses a flexible system for dynamically creating machine learning callbacks and loggers based on configuration settings. This system allows for the definition of various behaviors during model training and validation without requiring direct code modifications. The primary mechanism for this is provided by the [`instantiate_callbacks`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/instantiators.py#L19) and [`instantiate_loggers`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/instantiators.py#L47) utilities, both located in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/instantiators.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/instantiators.py).

These utilities are designed to process configuration dictionaries, typically sourced from Hydra, to construct [`BaseCallback`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py#L9) and [`Logger`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rf3/src/rf3/train.py#L36) objects respectively. Each item in the configuration is validated to ensure it specifies a target class or function for instantiation. If a configuration is malformed, an [`InstantiationError`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/instantiators.py#L13) is raised, providing clear feedback about incorrect setups. This approach promotes a highly configurable and extensible training environment where different callbacks and logging strategies can be easily swapped or combined via configuration files.

### Distributed Training Utilities and Logging
Utilities are available for setting up and managing Distributed Data Parallel (DDP) environments, including functions to determine the current process rank and check if it is the rank-zero process. The function [`set_accelerator_based_on_availability`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/ddp.py#L22) in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/ddp.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/ddp.py) automatically configures the accelerator settings within a training configuration based on available hardware, such as CUDA GPUs, Intel XPUs, or Apple MPS, ensuring appropriate [`accelerator`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/README.md#L40), [`devices_per_node`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/engine.py#L79), and [`num_nodes`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/engine.py#L78) are set. Additionally, a [`RankedLogger`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/ddp.py#L58) is provided for DDP-aware logging, which prefixes log messages with the current process's rank and supports rank-zero-only logging, preventing redundant output in distributed setups. See [Foundry Core Library and ML Workflows](#foundry-core-library-and-ml-workflows) for additional details.

### Intel XPU Support for PyTorch Lightning Fabric
The [`foundry.utils.xpu`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L38) module provides utilities for enabling and managing Intel XPU (GPU) devices within PyTorch Lightning Fabric applications. This support allows for XPU acceleration, single-device training strategies, and mixed precision operations on Intel GPUs.

The [`SingleXPUStrategy`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/xpu/single_xpu_strategy.py#L13) class, defined in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/xpu/single_xpu_strategy.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/xpu/single_xpu_strategy.py), extends Lightning's [`SingleDeviceStrategy`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/xpu/single_xpu_strategy.py#L9) to manage training and inference specifically on a single Intel XPU device. It ensures that Lightning Fabric components are configured and executed correctly on XPU, verifying device availability during initialization.

For managing interactions with Intel XPU devices, the [`XPUAccelerator`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/xpu/xpu_accelerator.py#L9) class in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/xpu/xpu_accelerator.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/xpu/xpu_accelerator.py) inherits from [`Accelerator`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L20). It handles device setup, parsing of device specifications, and reporting available XPU device counts, relying on [`torch.xpu`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/ddp.py#L39) functionalities.

Mixed precision training on Intel XPU devices is facilitated by the [`XPUMixedPrecision`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/xpu/xpu_precision.py#L11) class, located in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/xpu/xpu_precision.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/xpu/xpu_precision.py). This component enables automatic mixed precision (AMP) by using [`torch.autocast`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/trainer/rfd3.py#L92) during the model's forward pass, ensuring that computations are performed at the appropriate floating-point precision (e.g., [`torch.float16`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/xpu/xpu_precision.py#L33) or [`torch.bfloat16`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/xpu/xpu_precision.py#L35)).

These components are designed to allow [`Lightning Fabric`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rfd3/README.md#L150) [`Trainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/models/rf3/src/rf3/train.py#L92) instances to leverage Intel XPU devices for scalable and efficient model development. For further details on the [`FabricTrainer`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L56), see [Training Harness with PyTorch Lightning Fabric](#foundry-core-library-and-ml-workflows-training-harness-with-pytorch-lightning-fabric).

### Rigid Body Transformations and Geometric Augmentation
Foundry's deep learning infrastructure incorporates utilities for handling 3D rigid transformations, which are fundamental in structural bioinformatics models. These utilities, primarily found in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rigid.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rigid.py), abstract complex geometric operations, such as rotations and translations, for efficient manipulation of molecular coordinates within a deep learning framework.

The [`Rotation`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rigid.py#L278) class within [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rigid.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rigid.py) encapsulates 3D rotations, supporting both 3x3 rotation matrices and 4-element quaternions. It provides methods for composing rotations, applying them to 3D points, and inverting them. Similarly, the [`Rigid`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rigid.py#L850) class, also in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rigid.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rigid.py), combines a [`Rotation`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rigid.py#L278) object with a 3D translation vector to represent complete rigid transformations. This class supports composition with other rigid transformations, application to points, and inversion. Both classes offer conversions to and from common tensor representations, such as 4x4 homogeneous matrices or 7-element quaternion+translation vectors. A notable feature is the ability to construct a [`Rigid`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rigid.py#L850) transformation from three 3D points, which is used for defining local coordinate frames. These utilities are designed with robustness in mind, particularly for use with Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP) training, by implementing core matrix and vector multiplications to avoid potential numerical issues.

Complementing these rigid body transformations are geometric augmentation methods, located in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rotation_augmentation.py`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rotation_augmentation.py). These methods are used to introduce variability into training data by applying random rotations and translations to batches of atomic coordinates. This augmentation helps improve the generalization of models by exposing them to diverse orientations of molecular structures. Key functions include [`uniform_random_rotation`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rotation_augmentation.py#L37) for generating random rotation matrices and [`centre_random_augmentation`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/src/foundry/utils/rotation_augmentation.py#L30) which first centers atom coordinates and then applies random rotations and translations. This process is crucial for training models that are invariant to the global orientation and position of molecular complexes. For further details on how these utilities integrate into the broader training system, refer to [Training Harness and Distributed Training](#training-harness-and-distributed-training).

## Environment Setup and Examples
Foundry provides clear guidance for setting up development and execution environments, primarily through a reference [`Dockerfile`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/examples/docker/Dockerfile#L5) located in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/examples/docker/Dockerfile`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/examples/docker/Dockerfile). This Dockerfile streamlines the process of creating a custom Foundry image, simplifying environment configuration, dependency management, and base model downloads.

The Dockerfile employs a two-stage build process. The initial [`BUILDER`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/examples/docker/Dockerfile#L15) stage is responsible for setting up the comprehensive development environment. This includes installing system dependencies such as [`git`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/README.md#L33) and [`build-essential`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/examples/docker/Dockerfile#L24), creating a Python virtual environment, and installing Foundry with all its dependencies. Crucially, it also handles the download of base Foundry models into a designated [`checkpoints`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/.env#L62) directory. Following this, the final image stage copies the prepared environment, ensuring that the runtime image is optimized for execution while still including all necessary components and pre-downloaded models. The [`PATH`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/docs/make.bat#L19) environment variable is configured to allow direct execution of Foundry commands within the container.

### Dockerized Foundry Environment Setup
The Foundry project provides a reference [`Dockerfile`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/examples/docker/Dockerfile#L5) in [`/rosettacommons/foundry/examples/docker/Dockerfile`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/examples/docker/Dockerfile) to establish a Dockerized environment for development and execution. This Dockerfile employs a two-stage build process to optimize for both setup efficiency and runtime image size.

The initial stage, labeled [`BUILDER`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/examples/docker/Dockerfile#L15), is designed to prepare the complete development environment. It begins by installing system-level dependencies such as [`ca-certificates`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/examples/docker/Dockerfile#L21), [`git`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/README.md#L33), [`mc`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/examples/docker/Dockerfile#L23), and [`build-essential`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/examples/docker/Dockerfile#L24). Following this, it leverages [`uv`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/README.md#L26) to manage Python dependencies, creating a virtual environment, installing Foundry with all its requirements, and subsequently downloading base Foundry models into the [`/app/foundry/checkpoints`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/examples/docker/Dockerfile#L36) directory using the [`foundry install base-models`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/README.md#L1) command. This stage ensures that all necessary tools and model checkpoints are present before moving to the final image construction.

The second stage constructs the final, more compact runtime image. This stage copies only the essential artifacts from the [`BUILDER`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/examples/docker/Dockerfile#L15) stage—specifically, the configured [`/root`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/examples/docker/Dockerfile#L38) and [`/app`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/examples/docker/Dockerfile#L28) directories containing the Foundry installation and downloaded models. It also reinstalls minimal runtime system dependencies. The environment variables are set to include the Foundry virtual environment's executables in the system [`PATH`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/docs/make.bat#L19), making Foundry commands directly accessible. The working directory is set to [`/app/foundry`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/examples/docker/Dockerfile#L31), and the container is configured to launch with [`bash`](https://github.com/rosettacommons/foundry/README.md#L14), allowing users to interactively execute Foundry commands. This separation ensures that the final Docker image is optimized for deployment and execution, containing only what is strictly necessary for Foundry operations.
